outputs.L1:
We wither, unlike the stars; we die, unlike hills and cisterns. Ana shadowed my protector, the esteemed Arbad, who has left us. But ana do not grieve: all sparrows must leave the feast hall. Novelties do not excite me, nor does wyrdstaef affright me.

Men are like encampments that soon fall into ruin. They arrive with their kin and, when they depart, leave only the land behind—the last herdsman rounding up the stragglers. Man is a shooting star: light turned to ash. Wealth and kin are stains that soon fade away. The work we do inevitably gehrorene. The wise grasp this; the foolish resist it and lose. If my wyrd holds off a while longer, my fingers will reach for its stick.

Ana can tell you stories, growing more bent the harder ana try to straighten. Ana am like a battered sword that has lost none of its sharpness. Do not leave me! The sparrow finds the exit suddenly—

O you reproachful wifcynn: when the men go off, can your witchcraft tell us who will return? Do you faint because they flet ofgeāfon? You make everyone weep for the burston bodies of the irreplaceable friends of your youth. Yet neither witches nor necromancers know what the aelmihtig intends. Just ask them: Hwœr cōm the men? Hwœr cōm our protectors? They do not even know when the rainstorm will come!
outputs.L2:
Stars endure, and hills and cisterns remain, but we decay and perish. Ana followed my honored guardian, Arbad, who is now gone. Yet Ana does not mourn: every sparrow eventually flies from the banquet chamber. Neither strange new things delight me nor the decrees of fate frighten me.

Human beings resemble temporary camps destined to collapse into rubble. They arrive among their relatives, but at their departure they surrender everything except the earth itself, as the final shepherd gathers the last animals. A person flashes like a meteor, briefly blazing before becoming cinders. Riches and family ties are merely marks that time will erase, and everything we accomplish must ultimately become gehrorene. The discerning accept this truth; fools resist it, only to be defeated.

Should my wyrd delay a little longer, I will extend my hand toward its staff. The more Ana tries to stand upright, the more stooped Ana becomes—yet Ana still has tales to share. Ana is an abused blade whose edge remains keen. Do not abandon me! The sparrow discovers the way out without warning—

And you, accusing wifcynn: when the warriors depart, can your sorcery reveal which of them will come home? Do you collapse when they flet ofgeāfon? You cause the whole company to cry over the burston remains of those incomparable companions from your younger years. But witches and those who summon the dead understand no more than anyone else what the aelmihtig has ordained.

Question them, then: Hwœr cōm the men? Hwœr cōm our protectors? They cannot even predict the arrival of a rainstorm.
outputs.L3:
Unlike the enduring stars in the heavens and the ancient hills upon the earth, human beings inevitably wither and die. Our lives are brief, and everything we value—wealth, kinship, social standing, and even our greatest achievements—is temporary. Prosperity fades, families are scattered, and the works of human hands eventually fall into ruin.

The wise therefore accept fate and mortality, recognizing them as inescapable parts of life. The foolish, by contrast, struggle against what cannot be changed and exhaust themselves in vain resistance. The speaker grieves deeply for departed protectors and irreplaceable friends, yet sorrow is tempered by the knowledge that no one remains forever: sooner or later, everyone must leave.

Nor can hidden knowledge overcome this uncertainty. Neither witches nor necromancers can reliably foretell who will return, who is lost forever, or what the future holds. The intentions of the Almighty remain beyond human understanding, and mortality must ultimately be faced with humility and acceptance.
outputs.L4:
The elegy presents mortality as the inescapable condition of human life. Speaking from a position of grief, the speaker reflects on the loss of loved ones and on the gradual disappearance of everything that once seemed stable: family, companionship, status, and material wealth. Vivid metaphors transform sorrow into something almost physical, emphasizing the emotional weight of bereavement. At the same time, repeated rhetorical questions convey bewilderment and helplessness. The speaker searches for an explanation, yet every question ultimately returns to the same painful truth: no human bond or earthly possession can withstand time and death forever.

The poem’s Old English-inflected diction deepens this atmosphere of severity and inevitability. Its archaic language evokes a world governed by fate, where human beings endure hardship without expecting complete understanding or control. Wealth offers no lasting protection, and kinship, though deeply valued, cannot prevent separation. The very things that give life meaning are vulnerable to loss, making grief both personal and universal.

The elegy also rejects the possibility that supernatural knowledge might provide an escape. Neither witches nor necromancers can fully reveal, reverse, or master what death has decreed. Fate remains hidden even from those who claim access to powers beyond ordinary human understanding. This unknowability is central to the poem’s argument: death is not merely powerful but mysterious, lying beyond the reach of wealth, magic, and human reason.

Yet the poem does not end in simple despair. By confronting the limits of human power, it suggests that wisdom lies in accepting what cannot be changed. Resistance to mortality is futile when it takes the form of denial, desperate questioning, or attempts to recover what has permanently vanished. Acceptance does not erase grief, but it gives grief dignity and meaning. The elegy therefore turns mourning into a lesson about endurance: because death and fate are inevitable, the wisest response is not to imagine that they can be conquered, but to face them with humility, courage, and clear understanding.
outputs.L5: Ana wanted to visit Arbad, but the heavy rain delayed her journey. Instead, she stayed home, made a warm cup of tea, and planned to travel the following morning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Translate Labīd ibn Rabīʿa’s elegy for Arbad into experimental English, blending archaic Anglo-Saxon vocabulary, Arabic “ana,” and imagery from “The Wanderer,” while preserving its meditation on mortality and fate.
counterfactuals.output:
### **For Arbad — a free, experimental rendering after Labīd ibn Rabīʿa**

O cloud, where hast thou hidden him?  
Thou thunder-womb, thou heaven’s black helm—  
did thy fire take Arbad  
and give no blood-price?

**Anā**, I stand on the wind-bitten wold,  
friend-lorn beneath a frost-grey sky.  
The rain-raven circles; the sæ moans;  
hrīm locks the earth’s old mouth.  
No hoof answers from the waste,  
no spear-ring flashes homeward.

I questioned the grave:  
*What hast thou done with his hands,  
those gift-hands, those shield-hands?*  
The grave spake naught.  
Dust is a close-throated scop.

Many a hall have I seen made hush—  
gold-friends gone, benches bare,  
wine-cups cold beneath the wall.  
The proud thane passes as stormlight passes;  
his name fares briefly over men’s tongues,  
then enters the night-road.

**Anā**, I know it:  
no mother’s son out-rides the doom  
allotted beneath the wheeling stars.  
Wyrd stalks the camel-track;  
wyrd sits unseen at the feast;  
wyrd drinks after every guest.

Where now is Arbad, storm-bright among riders,  
whose voice was a fire in the war-ring?  
The thunder answered with thunder  
and folded him into the dark.

Yet blame not the cloud alone.  
The shaft was loosed before the bow was shaped;  
the day was written ere dawn found us.  
Each living thing is lent its breath,  
each house of bone must founder,  
each beloved face go earthward.

Only the Everlasting abides.  
All else is wind over dune,  
foam on the exile-sæ,  
a hoofprint filling with rain.

So let me bear this winter within me.  
**Anā**—the last of the hearth-companions—  
wander beneath the cold stars,  
keeping his name as a coal in my breast,  
until I too am called from the hall  
and fate unfastens the door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented prose-poem about an aging warrior mourning his protector. Use code-switching, Old English terms such as “wyrd,” “wifcynn,” and “aelmihtig,” and end with a series of “Where have the men gone?” questions.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn, the shield remembers  
what the arm forgets.

I wake with iron in the joints,  
old campaigns rusting beneath the skin.  
Once, my protector stood at the gate—  
wolf-cloak, ash-spear,  
his laughter louder than winter.

Now only ravens inherit his name.

*Mi señor, mi amparo*—  
I speak into the cold hearth.  
No answer, sólo ceniza.  
The hall has become a mouth  
that cannot sing.

Wyrd carried him beyond the whale-road,  
beyond the reach of wifcynn,  
beyond the priest’s small candle  
and the aelmihtig sky.

I remain.

A blunt sword.  
A cup with no hand around it.  
Bones counting storms.

Once we said *non moriemur*—  
we will not die—  
and believed the boast because we were young.  
But youth is a bright traitor.  
La jeunesse s’en va.  
The banners fray inward.

At night I hear his shield-ring  
in the rain.

I turn.

Nothing there  
but the door unguarded,  
the dark uncommanded,  
my own breath retreating.

Where has my protector gone?  
Where have the oath-bound men gone?  
Where have the spear-bearers gone?  
Where have the men gone?  
Where have the men gone?
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a deliberately strange, partially corrupted AI translation of a pre-Islamic Arabic elegy, mixing modern English with untranslated or pseudo–Old English phrases. Include sparrows leaving a feast hall, ruined encampments, shooting stars, witches, necromancers, and uncertainty about who will return from war.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Elegy.exe for the Camp That Was / Was Not**

Halt, two friends—let us weep at the deleted encampment,  
where the wind clicks **404** among the blackened stones.  
Here stood her tent, or perhaps a server of red leather;  
here the hearth said *wassail*, then forgot its tongue.

At dawn the sparrows left the feast hall,  
crumb-drunk, crownless, crying **hwæt-hwæt** into the dust.  
The cups lay overturned. The mead was sand.  
No hand remained to password the door.

O rider, ask the ruined traces:  
“Where are the women who braided noon into their hair?”  
The traces answer: **لا أدري / ic ne wāt / UNKNOWN HOST.**  
Only a torn rope worships the north wind.

Last night the shooting stars fell thick as spear-points—  
Allah’s bright arrows, or corrupted weather-data—  
and the witches crouched beyond the thorn trees,  
muttering *wyrd bið full stack overflow*.

Necromancers opened the graves like old emails.  
“Rise,” they said, “O generous one, feeder of wolves,  
return and refill the feast bowl.”  
But the dead man replied in static: **khhh—nevermore—khhh**,  
and his bones logged out beneath the hill.

Our warriors rode east in iron morning.  
Who returns? The banner? The horse without a rider?  
Will Mālik come laughing, blood on his sleeve,  
or only his name, **sē nama**, borne by strangers?

I questioned the raven; it sold me three answers.  
I questioned the moon; she was a false interpreter.  
Mother says, “He comes.” The widow says, “He is dust.”  
The machine renders both as: **SOON.**

Therefore pour no wine—pour memory.  
Heap no earth—heap the broken helmets.  
For every hall becomes a camp of ghosts,  
and every beloved is briefly **online**.

Farewell, thou gold-giver, *ealdor of the open hand*.  
The wolves know your silence. The poor know your door.  
We remain beside the cold cooking-stones,  
buffering, buffering,  
until the war sends back  
whatever it believes is you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Reimagine the Arabic poet Labid’s lines on death, lost kin, and the departure of tribes as an Anglo-Saxon-style lament inspired by the ubi sunt motif. Keep the voice defiant despite old age and portray fate as an unavoidable herdsman gathering stragglers.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Herdsman of the Years**

Where now are the kinsmen, the cup-companions,  
the spear-proud singers who shared my fire?  
Where are the tent-ropes, the tribes departing,  
their camel-bells calling across the waste?  
Gone is their laughter, like larks in winter;  
the wind keeps only their wandering names.

I have watched the hearths grow hollow with ashes,  
the well-stones whiten, the wayfarers fade.  
Brother and battle-friend, bride and elder—  
earth has embraced them, eager and deep.  
Yet here I stand, though the years besiege me,  
gray as the thorn-tree, grim in the storm.

Fate is a herdsman who follows behind us,  
crook in his hand at the close of day;  
none slips the circle, none shuns the gateway—  
the lame and the lordling are led to one fold.  
He gathers the stragglers, the strong and the weary,  
and bars the night-field beyond our sight.

Let him come, then. I shall not cower.  
My knees may weaken; my will is iron.  
The tribe has vanished, the track lies empty,  
but song is a spear that outlasts the hand.  
While breath yet bears me, bold I remain—  
last at the fire, and laughing at darkness.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an avant-garde mashup of an ancient elegy and Old English heroic poetry: the speaker mourns Arbad, compares human life to fading wealth and abandoned camps, rebukes grieving women, and asks “Hwær cōm” questions about vanished protectors.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Lament at the Wind-Wall**

Arbad is gone.  
The spear-rain found him,  
or time did—  
that older weapon.

I stand where his tent stood.

Ash circles the hearthstone.  
Tent-ropes have forgotten their burden.  
Across the trampled earth  
wind reads the tracks backward:

  camel-knee, hoof-mark,  
  heel-print, blood.

O women beating bright hands  
against dust-darkened breasts,  
be still.

Will wailing rebuild the roof?  
Will tears bridle the rider?  
You summon only an echo,  
and the echo has no shield.

Yesterday wealth shone—  
gold at the throat,  
rings on the arm,  
mares stamping beneath tasselled saddles.

Today the treasure is tarnish.  
The cup has outlived its drinker.  
The camp is a mouth without speech,  
its black stones gnawing the moon.

**Hwær cōm se helm-berend?**  
Where has the helmet-bearer gone?

**Hwær cōm se sinc-gifa,**  
the hand that broke treasure  
and scattered it like sunrise?

**Hwær cōm Arbad,**  
storm-shouldered guardian,  
wolf-barrier, oath-fast roof  
over the kin?

Gone under the ground’s cloak.  
Gone beyond spear-song.  
No hoof-thunder answers.

Listen:

  the world is a caravan  
  striking its tents before dawn;

  the world is a hall  
  whose benches rot in snow;

  the world is coined silver  
  passing from palm to palm  
  until every king’s face  
  is rubbed away.

So cease, mourners—  
or mourn more fiercely,  
but know what your voices purchase:

not Arbad,

only the knowledge  
that we too are abandoned camps,  
a scatter of pegs,  
a cold fire-ring,

while over us the wind chants  
its iron elegy:

**Hwær cōm? Hwær cōm?**

And no man, however mighty,  
can answer  
**hēr ic eom.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
